recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Bio: Kyle Denton is a community herbalist and medicine maker from Wisconsin who founded Tippecanoe Herbs with his wife Serena Marinelli in 2015. From their Milwaukee apothecary they craft small batch remedies from locally harvested and organic herbs, working from a bio terrain philosophy that blends Ayurveda with Western herbalism. He also runs Root Radical Herbal Academy, has taught for over a decade through his annual three season class and his Milwaukee herb walks, and sees clients as the Tuning Herbalist, using tuning forks to read the biofield. His Substack and podcast, Resonature, explore the interval between vital herbalism, biofield tuning and cosmology.
recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Name: Kyle Denton
recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Role: Community herbalist, founder of Tippecanoe Herbs

fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Botanical Power Couple Behind Tippecanoe Herbs", "body": "Chance introduces Kyle Denton, the returning guest he calls the show's court herbalist and fairy folk ambassador, alongside his wife Serena Marinelli in her first appearance. Together they run Tippecanoe Herbs, the Milwaukee shop that grew out of farmers market booths. Serena describes the division of labor with affection: Kyle is the Aquarius, the creative, the wizard, the druid who makes concoctions, while she is the Sagittarius who says let's make it real and gets a label on the bottle. Before they combined forces she was living in Italy and he was in Wisconsin. Their son Davide arrived after the shop, which they call their first born."}, {"title": "Fertility As A Conversation For Two", "body": "Serena opens the fertility discussion by pushing back on the assumption that conception is the woman's problem alone, saying it takes two and that the responsibility of creation should be shared. Kyle describes what he sees at the shop counter, where a woman approaches with a question while her partner waits on what they affectionately call the boyfriend couch, a little chair off in the corner. Kyle says the practice he likes to preserve is having that conversation with both partners present, and he contends that the man's own state of health is part of the picture, a turn in the conversation the boyfriend rarely expects."}, {"title": "Doctrine Of Signatures And Plant Lore", "body": "A large share of the episode is Kyle's interpretive method rather than any protocol. He reads plants through what he calls his astro herbal chart, assigning them to Venus, Mars, the Moon or Virgo, and pairing every Venusian softness with a Martian counterpart, because where there is a princess there is always a prince, the thorn and the bramble. He layers in the alchemical triad of salt, sulfur and mercury and the principles of three. He also detours into folklore, noting that Achillea takes its name from Achilles, taught by the centaur Chiron, and calling the old leaves of three warning a psyop against learning to identify poison ivy."}, {"title": "Grief, Identity And The Passage To Motherhood", "body": "The most personal stretch is Serena on what changes in a woman after loss or after birth. She frames the postpartum shift as a question of identity: you once were a maiden, now you are a mother, so you have lost what you were before, grieving a self you knew while meeting a newer self you do not know yet, becoming a stranger to yourself. The heartbeat, she says, is the rhythm of the present moment, an answer to a mind stuck in what if. In the outro Chance and his wife Jennifer speak about their own loss the previous year and how many women quietly wrote to her afterward."}, {"title": "The Father To Be, Flower Essences And Whole Plants", "body": "Chance asks what supports the man taking on the mantle of fatherhood, and Kyle answers with categories rather than prescriptions. He defines adaptogens as plants said to help every system adapt to stress, then spends time on Wisconsin's American ginseng industry near Wausau, which he describes as heavily pesticided and expensive, arguing for a trusted organic grower. He praises a flower essence called Truth Teller, labeled conviction, and describes what a man running a business pushes down instead of saying. Kyle also makes a craft case against essential oils, noting it takes forty roses to make a single drop, preferring whole plants in carrier oils."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Husband and wife super-duo Kyle Denton & Serena Marinelli join InnerVerse to talk about herbalism strategies for the stages of motherhood. Through their company, Tippecanoe Herbs, Kyle and Serena spread the sage wisdom of plant power and provide many products for life-enhancement. In the free hour, we discuss fertility, conception and pregnancy, and what herbal allies are equipped to nourish and relieve women through these exciting steps.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension, we continue addressing various aspects of pregnancy, herbs for stimulating labor, the man's role in preparing and guiding the birth process, bringing consciousness to contractions, healing after baby comes, post-partum plants, enhancing breast milk production & nutrition, breaking generational trauma conditioning, and much more!

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Gentle Hands and the Body's Own Will", "body": "The members' hour opens in the second trimester, where Serena favors self massage, dry brushing and bodywork as a mother's balance shifts around the weight she carries, drawing on her own visits to a chiropractor. The couple joke about the crack and go showman style and steer listeners toward practitioners who work specifically with pregnant women and children, and away from deep tissue work. Chance adds that the best modalities enforce no external will on the body and instead support it in expressing its own, which brings craniosacral work into the conversation, along with the quality of hydration, spring water and fresh local summer produce."}, {"title": "Salt, Silica and Real Food", "body": "Serena recommends Lily Nichols' book Real Food for Pregnancy, described as research minded without being heavy, half cookbook, and willing to dismantle old diet myths such as the fear of salt. From there the pair reframe salt as minerals: water follows salt, and the salty flavor herbalists talk about is the taste of mineral richness, not greasy spoon diner salt. Kyle extends the idea to oat straw, whose dried stems glint like shards of selenite because of their silica, the mineral that lets a plant blow in the wind without breaking, and he explains why a long steeped infusion draws out minerals that a tincture does not."}, {"title": "A Father's Preparation", "body": "A couples' pregnancy class asked everyone to rank what mattered most, and Serena recalls the women putting the birth itself first while the men chose financial stability and the mother's safety. Kyle's preparation was unexpected: months studying law, learning to write an affidavit and a statement of truth and having them notarized, so that if their home birth plan changed nobody would separate the family or act without his agreement. Signing, he says, felt like a spiritual shift, as if God had been waiting for his name. His aim was to be the rock, and Serena stresses talking through wishes beforehand so both partners are on the same page."}, {"title": "Surrender and the Strong Feeling", "body": "The herbalists laugh that Kyle left the prepared birth herbs at the shop, and both say the baby came only once they gave up their own will and said, it is your plan, God, a moment the three agree is a microcosm for life. Serena describes refusing the script that birth must mean suffering: a contraction is a strong feeling rather than a painful one, and the space between is a peace to be thankful for. She calls birth a rite of passage in which her maiden self dies as the baby is born. Chance relays Elise of Family Fungi's image of natural birth as a psychopomp journey in reverse."}, {"title": "Life After Birth and Broken Conditioning", "body": "They admit they prepared for fertility, pregnancy and birth but not for what came after, and Serena compares it to acing one exam only to find there is no break before the next. She describes the first forty days, when mother and baby are one, a kitchen with a different pot on every burner, freezer meals made months ahead, and family and friends bringing food. Kyle urges fathers to drop their ideals and offer solutions rather than burden their partners, and tells how laughing off a snotty kiss showed him he had broken a generational fear of germs. Serena closes by calling birth the real rebellious act."}]
